title: The history of MRI
tagline: From an Irish physicist's wobbling charges in 1897 to 11.7-tesla images of the living brain.
intro: Physicists spent half a century learning that atomic nuclei are tiny magnets that can be flipped by radio waves. Then, in the 1970s, doctors and chemists asked whether those signals could find disease, and a few inventors worked out how to turn them into pictures. Within a decade MRI was in hospitals, and today it can even watch the brain think.

eras.name: The spinning nucleus
eras.summary: Physicists discover that nuclei are tiny magnets that wobble in a field, and that radio waves can flip them.

eras.name: Resonance in the lab
eras.summary: NMR is found in ordinary matter and becomes a chemist's tool. Echoes and relaxation times are measured, and tissues turn out to differ.

eras.name: From signals to pictures
eras.summary: Gradients, slices and Fourier transforms turn NMR signals into images, first of tubes, then of a finger, then of a whole person.

eras.name: Into the hospital
eras.summary: Superconducting scanners go on sale, contrast agents arrive, and MRI spreads around the world.

eras.name: Watching the brain
eras.summary: Diffusion and blood-oxygen imaging let MRI follow water in nerve fibres and see which brain areas are working.

eras.name: Stronger, safer, lighter
eras.summary: Fields climb to 7 T and beyond, safety rules tighten, and low-helium and portable scanners widen access.

events.title: A spinning charge wobbles in a field
events.text: Studying how magnets change the light from atoms, the Irish physicist Joseph Larmor showed that charges circling in a magnetic field precess: they wobble round the field at a rate set by its strength.
events.why: That wobble, now called Larmor precession, is the frequency every MRI scanner tunes its radio to.

events.title: Blood is magnetic, when it has no oxygen
events.text: Measuring haemoglobin in a magnetic field, Pauling and Coryell found that it is weakly repelled when it carries oxygen, but weakly pulled in when it has given the oxygen up.
events.why: Fifty-four years later this difference became the BOLD signal that lets fMRI watch the brain at work.

events.title: Two near misses
events.text: In 1936 the Dutch physicist Cornelis Gorter tried to detect nuclear magnetic resonance in solids and failed. Around 1941 Yevgeny Zavoisky in Kazan saw signals that may have been NMR, but the field of his magnet was not uniform enough to repeat them reliably. In 1944 he discovered the related electron spin resonance instead.
events.why: The effect was real but faint, and finding it needed better magnets and radio electronics.

events.title: Resonance in a beam of molecules
events.text: At Columbia University, Rabi sent a beam of molecules through magnets and a radio-frequency field. At one exact frequency the nuclei flipped and the beam went astray: magnetic resonance. It won him the 1944 Nobel Prize in Physics.
events.why: It proved nuclei can be flipped by radio waves at a frequency set by the field.

events.title: NMR in ordinary matter
events.text: Two teams, working separately, found the signal in everyday materials. Purcell's group at Harvard saw it in paraffin wax on 15 December 1945, and Bloch's group at Stanford saw it in water in January 1946. They shared the 1952 Nobel Prize in Physics.
events.why: For the first time the hydrogen in a lump of matter, or a body, could be made to give a radio signal.

events.title: The spin echo
events.text: Hahn hit spins with two short radio pulses and heard an unexpected extra signal afterwards: an echo, as the fanned-out spins came back into step.
events.why: Spin echoes are still at the heart of many MRI scans, and they let scientists measure T2.

events.title: Living tissue gives different signals
events.text: After visiting Bloch at Stanford, the Swedish doctor Erik Odeblad built his own NMR equipment and measured human tissues and body fluids. He found that their relaxation times differ.
events.why: It was an early hint that NMR could tell one tissue from another.

events.title: An imaging idea filed away
events.text: Soviet records credit Vladislav Ivanov, a young air-force officer, with applying for an inventor's certificate for a way to image the inside of objects with magnetic resonance. It was rejected as unrealistic and only granted in 1984.
events.why: It shows the idea of MR imaging was in the air long before the first pictures.

events.title: Tumours relax more slowly
events.text: At the State University of New York Downstate, Damadian reported in Science that tumours in rats had longer NMR relaxation times than healthy tissue. He proposed using NMR to detect cancer and patented a scanning idea, granted in 1974.
events.why: It pointed NMR towards medicine and showed that T1 and T2 could reveal disease.

events.title: The first MR image
events.text: Lauterbur had the idea over dinner in 1971: add a gradient so the field, and the frequency, change with position. Nature first rejected his paper, then published it in 1973 with an image of two small tubes of water. He called the method zeugmatography.
events.why: Gradients turned a signal into a picture, and every MRI since uses them.

events.title: Slices and k-space
events.text: At the University of Nottingham, Mansfield's group described NMR 'diffraction', the forerunner of k-space, in 1973, and a way to excite just one slice with a gradient in 1974.
events.why: Slice selection lets a scanner image one thin section of the body at a time.

events.title: Pictures by Fourier transform
events.who: Anil Kumar, Dieter Welti and Richard Ernst
events.text: At ETH Zurich, Ernst's group showed how to build MR images with phase and frequency encoding and a Fourier transform. Ernst won the 1991 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on NMR methods.
events.why: Nearly every clinical scanner still fills k-space and uses a Fourier transform this way.

events.title: The first image of a living human part
events.text: Mansfield and Maudsley published cross-sections of a living human finger, made in 1976. The same year Mansfield described echo-planar imaging, a way to make a whole picture from a single pulse in a fraction of a second.
events.why: Echo-planar imaging later made fMRI and diffusion scans possible.

events.title: Indomitable scans a person
events.text: Damadian's team built a superconducting scanner they named Indomitable. Graduate student Larry Minkoff sat inside for nearly five hours while it gathered 106 points, one at a time, to make a rough cross-section of his chest. The machine is now in the Smithsonian's collection.
events.why: It was the first MR scan of a whole human body.

events.title: The first useful patient scan
events.text: The University of Aberdeen's home-built Mark-One scanner, with a 0.04 T magnet, scanned a man with cancer and revealed a tumour in his spine that other tests had not found. It went on to scan thousands of patients.
events.why: It showed MRI could change what doctors did for a patient.

events.title: Scanners go on sale
events.who: FONAR, EMI and Picker, GE, and others
events.text: FONAR offered the first commercial whole-body scanner around 1980–81. At Hammersmith Hospital in London, a team from EMI made the first series of brain images in 1981, and GE showed 1.5 T images in 1983. The US FDA approved the first MRI systems for sale in 1984.
events.why: MRI moved from physics labs into hospitals.

events.title: India's first MRI scanner
events.who: Institute of Nuclear Medicine and Allied Sciences (INMAS, DRDO)
events.text: The first MRI scanner in India was installed at INMAS in Delhi; sources give 1986 or 1987. AIIMS in New Delhi got its first clinical 1.5 T scanner in 1993.
events.why: It began MRI for patients in a country where scanners are now found in cities across the country.

events.title: Imaging water on the move
events.text: Le Bihan showed how to make MR images of diffusion, the random wandering of water molecules. In 1994, with Peter Basser at the US National Institutes of Health, he introduced diffusion tensor imaging, which measures the direction water moves most easily.
events.why: Diffusion scans now spot strokes within minutes and trace the brain’s wiring.

events.title: A contrast agent for MRI
events.where: Berlin, Germany; approved in the USA
events.text: Gadopentetate dimeglumine, sold as Magnevist, was approved in the United States as the first gadolinium contrast agent for MRI. Injected into a vein, it shortens T1 and makes some tumours and inflamed areas stand out.
events.why: Contrast agents made MRI better at finding disease that plain scans miss.

events.title: Blood oxygen lights up the brain
events.text: At AT&T Bell Laboratories, Ogawa showed in rats that the amount of oxygen in blood changes the MR signal near vessels. He called it blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) contrast.
events.why: BOLD is the signal behind almost every fMRI study of the working brain.

events.title: The first human fMRI
events.who: Peter Bandettini, Kenneth Kwong, Seiji Ogawa and teams
events.text: Three groups published within weeks of each other in 1992, showing the human visual and motor cortex lighting up as people looked at flashing lights or moved their fingers.
events.why: It opened a new science of mapping human thought without surgery or radiation.

events.title: 3 T comes to the clinic
events.text: Whole-body 3 T scanners were cleared by the US FDA for clinical use between about 1999 and 2002, doubling the field of the common 1.5 T machines.
events.why: Twice the field gives more signal, so sharper or faster scans, especially of the brain.

events.title: A tragedy changes safety rules
events.text: A six-year-old boy having an MRI scan was fatally injured when a steel oxygen cylinder was pulled into the magnet. The American College of Radiology published its first MR safety guidance the next year.
events.why: It is why MRI units now screen everyone and everything that goes near the magnet.

events.title: A Nobel Prize, and a protest
events.text: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Lauterbur and Mansfield for their discoveries concerning MRI. Damadian was left out. Supporters of Damadian ran full-page newspaper advertisements arguing that he should have shared it. The prize can go to at most three people, and the committee’s discussions stay sealed for 50 years.
events.why: It recognised imaging with gradients, and left a lasting debate about who deserves credit.

events.title: 7 T scanners approved for patients
events.text: The MAGNETOM Terra became the first 7 T scanner cleared for clinical use: in Europe in August 2017 and by the US FDA on 12 October 2017, for the head and limbs.
events.why: Ultra-high fields reach finer detail, such as tiny lesions in the brain.

events.title: A magnet that barely needs helium
events.text: Helium is scarce and its price swings with shortages. Philips' sealed BlueSeal 1.5 T magnet holds about 7 litres instead of about 1,500, with no quench pipe. In 2021 Siemens' 0.55 T MAGNETOM Free.Max was cleared with less than a litre.
events.why: Low-helium magnets make MRI cheaper to run and easier to install.

events.title: MRI on wheels
events.text: The US FDA cleared the first portable MRI scanner, which runs on a 0.064 T permanent magnet and a normal power socket and can be wheeled to a patient's bedside.
events.why: Low-field scanners could bring MRI to places that cannot house a giant magnet.

events.title: Made-in-India scanners
events.text: The Bengaluru start-up VoxelGrids unveiled a 1.5 T scanner in 2023 and installed its first clinical system in Chandrapur, Maharashtra, in December 2025. A government project led by SAMEER is building another 1.5 T system for AIIMS Delhi. Both have been called India's first indigenous MRI.
events.why: Home-grown scanners could make MRI far cheaper for Indian hospitals.

events.title: The strongest human MRI
events.text: The Iseult scanner, with an 11.7 T magnet, released its first images of the living human brain from 20 volunteers, showing detail 0.2 mm across.
events.why: Stronger fields keep pushing how finely MRI can see the brain.

series.title: Field strength of landmark human MRI scanners
series.caption: The magnets used to image people, from Indomitable's weak field to the 11.7 T Iseult. Most hospital scanners today are 1.5 or 3 T.

points.label: Ohio State University: first human images at 8 T
University of Minnesota: first human scans at 10.5 T
Iseult, France: first human brain images at 11.7 T

facts: A 1.5 T scanner's field is about 30,000 times stronger than Earth's, and it stays on day and night, even when nobody is being scanned.
A conventional 1.5 T magnet holds around 1,500 litres of liquid helium. Boiled into gas at room temperature, each litre swells to about 750 litres.
The first whole-body scan, in 1977, took nearly five hours to make one rough picture. Echo-planar imaging can now make a brain image in a fraction of a second.
MRI scanners can be louder than 110 decibels, about as loud as a rock concert, because the gradient coils flex in the magnet's field.
Japan has about 60 MRI scanners per million people, one of the highest rates in the OECD; the UK has about 9.
